channel_voice_profile: Clear, practical and conversational. Address the viewer directly; use complete sentences, explain unfamiliar terms, avoid hype, unsupported claims and invented personal experience.
topic: Git staging versus committing: choose what goes into one snapshot
angle: Teach a beginner with two changed files to commit only one. Show status, stage a named example file, inspect the staged diff, commit, then check what remains. Explain the index/working-tree distinction. Use hypothetical labels only; do not imply Git was executed.

sources.title: Git status reference
sources.author: Git project
sources.excerpt: git status reports staged changes for the next commit, unstaged working-tree changes, and untracked files.

sources.title: Git add reference
sources.author: Git project
sources.excerpt: git add followed by a path adds that file’s current contents to the index, the staging area used to prepare the next commit.

sources.title: Git diff reference
sources.author: Git project
sources.excerpt: git diff --cached shows changes staged for the next commit compared with HEAD; --staged is a synonym.

sources.title: Git commit reference
sources.author: Git project
sources.excerpt: git commit with a message records the current index contents as a new commit. In its basic form, it does not include unstaged working-tree changes.

notes: Use a hypothetical repository with app.py and notes.txt changed. The example paths are illustrative, not source facts or observed output.

Show git status, git add app.py, git diff --cached, git commit -m "Update app", and git status again as an intentional sequence. Do not fabricate command output, commit IDs, or an actual execution result.
Explain that staging app.py does not stage notes.txt and that the basic git commit form records the staged contents.
Use concrete visual contrast between working tree, index and commit. Reserve the bottom of the portrait frame for captions.
